chapters.title: The making of the modern world

points.title: Imperialism
points.brief: Imperialism is one country taking control of other lands and peoples. By 1914 European powers, Britain above all, ruled much of Africa, Asia and the Pacific.

points.title: Movements of people from 1750 to 1914
points.brief: Millions moved in this period, some forced, such as enslaved Africans and transported convicts, and many free, seeking land, gold or work in new countries.

points.title: The Atlantic slave trade and abolition
points.brief: Millions of Africans were shipped to the Americas as slaves. Campaigns by enslaved people and reformers led Britain to end the trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833.

points.title: Nationalism
points.brief: Nationalism is the belief that people who share a language, history and culture should rule themselves as a nation. It united Germany and Italy and later fed the rivalry that led to war.

points.title: Reliability and usefulness compared
points.brief: A source can be unreliable yet still useful. A one-sided recruiting poster is poor evidence of what war was like but good evidence of how the government wanted people to see it.

points.title: Short-term and long-term effects in history
points.brief: Effects can be short-term, such as deaths in a battle, or long-term, such as changed beliefs about a nation that last for generations.

points.title: Contested interpretations
points.brief: Historians sometimes disagree strongly about the past, such as how to describe frontier conflict, because they use different evidence, questions or values.

points.title: Writing a thesis statement
points.brief: A thesis is a one-sentence answer to the question that takes a clear position. Every paragraph of a historical argument then supports it with evidence.

units.title: Making and transforming the Australian nation

points.title: Why Britain colonised Australia
points.brief: After losing its American colonies, Britain needed somewhere to send convicts, and a base in the Pacific. The First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove in 1788.

points.title: Terra nullius
points.brief: Britain claimed the land as if it belonged to no one, an idea later called terra nullius, and made no treaty with its owners. The High Court rejected the idea in the Mabo case in 1992.

points.title: Effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians
points.brief: Disease such as smallpox, the loss of land, water and food sources, and violence devastated First Nations communities as settlement spread.

points.title: Frontier conflict and resistance
points.brief: First Nations Australians resisted the taking of their land, led by people such as Pemulwuy and Windradyne. Settlers and police carried out massacres, such as at Myall Creek in 1838.

points.title: Protection policies
points.brief: From the late 1800s, colonial laws let protectors control where First Nations Australians lived, worked and married, and remove children from their families.

points.title: Squatters and the wool industry
points.brief: Squatters took up huge areas of land for sheep, and wool became the colonies' main export, pushing settlement inland.

points.title: The gold rushes
points.brief: Gold found in 1851 drew hundreds of thousands of migrants, including many from China, and made the colonies richer and larger. Hostility to Chinese miners led to riots.

points.title: The Eureka Stockade
points.brief: In 1854 miners at Ballarat protested costly licences and their lack of a vote. Soldiers crushed the stockade, but miners soon won the vote.

points.title: Federation
points.brief: On 1 January 1901 the six colonies joined as the Commonwealth of Australia, for shared defence, free trade between the colonies and a national identity.

points.title: The White Australia policy
points.brief: The Immigration Restriction Act of 1901, one of the first federal laws, used a dictation test to keep out non-European migrants.

points.title: Votes for women and early reforms
points.brief: South Australian women won the vote in 1894 and women won the federal vote in 1902, though most First Nations people were shut out. An aged pension and a basic wage soon followed.

chapters.title: Causes and the call to arms

points.title: The long-term causes of the First World War
points.brief: Militarism, rival alliances, imperial competition and nationalism raised tensions among Europe's great powers before 1914.

points.title: The spark in 1914
points.brief: The killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in June 1914 set off a chain of declarations of war through the alliance system.

points.title: Why Australians enlisted
points.brief: Australians joined up out of loyalty to Britain, a sense of adventure, steady pay, and pressure from family and friends, all as volunteers.

points.title: First Nations soldiers
points.brief: Over a thousand First Nations Australians served, even though rules often barred them. Many found fairer treatment in the army than at home, but lost it on returning.

points.title: The Gallipoli landing
points.brief: On 25 April 1915 Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli in Turkey, aiming to open a sea route to Russia, but were held on the steep coast.

points.title: The Gallipoli campaign
points.brief: After eight months of fighting, disease and harsh conditions, with about 8,700 Australians dead, the troops were evacuated in December 1915.

points.title: Trench warfare on the Western Front
points.brief: In France and Belgium both sides dug long lines of trenches. Machine guns, artillery and gas made attacks across no man's land very costly.

points.title: Fromelles, Pozières and the Somme
points.brief: In 1916, at Fromelles and Pozières during the Battle of the Somme, Australians lost more men in weeks than in the whole Gallipoli campaign.

points.title: The Light Horse in the Middle East
points.brief: Australian Light Horse troops fought the Ottoman Empire in Sinai and Palestine, including the charge at Beersheba in 1917.

points.title: The Armistice
points.brief: With its allies collapsing and its army pushed back, Germany agreed to the Armistice, and fighting stopped at 11 am on 11 November 1918.

chapters.title: The home front and remembering the war

points.title: The conscription referendums
points.brief: Prime Minister Hughes twice asked voters to allow conscription for overseas service, in 1916 and 1917. Both were defeated and the issue split the nation.

points.title: Propaganda and censorship
points.brief: The government used posters and newspapers to urge enlistment and censored letters and news so people would keep supporting the war.

points.title: Women and the war
points.brief: Women served as nurses overseas, raised money, knitted and packed supplies, and campaigned both for and against conscription.

points.title: German Australians in wartime
points.brief: Under the War Precautions Act, thousands of people of German background were interned, and German place names were changed.

points.title: Returned soldiers
points.brief: Many soldiers came home wounded or with shell shock. Soldier settlement schemes gave them farms, but many failed on poor land.

points.title: The Anzac legend
points.brief: The Anzac legend praises mateship, courage and endurance. Historians debate whom it leaves out, such as women and First Nations soldiers, and how much it shaped national identity.

points.title: Why it began in Britain
points.brief: Britain had coal and iron, money to invest, an empire for raw materials and markets, and new farming methods that freed workers for towns.

points.title: Steam power and factories
points.brief: Improved steam engines, such as James Watt's, powered machines in factories, especially for cotton, and later trains and ships.

points.title: Working conditions and child labour
points.brief: Factory and mine workers, including young children, worked long hours for low pay in dangerous conditions.

points.title: Cities and public health
points.brief: Crowded cities grew fast, and dirty water spread diseases such as cholera until sewers and clean water supplies were built.

points.title: New ideas and reforms
points.brief: Capitalism, socialism and the Chartist push for working men's votes grew from industrial change, and Factory Acts began to limit working hours.
